title: Great speeches need good ideas
gist: Yglesias proposes a mechanical candidate-selection rule for Democrats — promote state legislators and downballot officials who electorally overperform — and documents the enormous unrecognized gap between Rashida Tlaib's and Ilhan Omar's district performance. He then argues Democrats, as the educated people's party, overrate the literary quality of speeches over content, using Obama's 2004 convention text as an example of substance no contemporary Democrat would voice.

insights.claim: Democrats would be in a much better position if the default House candidate-selection strategy were 'find a state legislator who overperforms' and the default Senate and gubernatorial strategy were 'find a House member or downballot statewide officeholder who overperforms.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A concrete, measurable screen for handicapping candidate quality and therefore Senate/House control probabilities, independent of national polling.
insights.locator: We're like a million light-years from this being the case

insights.claim: A second-order benefit of an overperformance-based selection rule is that it would give ambitious backbench politicians in safe seats a reason to actually care about electoral performance.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Identifies the incentive channel through which a party could raise candidate quality at scale — the mechanism to watch for evidence of actual party reform.
insights.quote: One reason this would be good is it would encourage ambitious backbench politicians in safe seats to actually care about electoral performance.
insights.locator: One reason this would be good

insights.claim: Past electoral performance is treated as a decent, though not guaranteed, indicator of future political success — the empirical basis for the whole selection rule.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Sets the epistemic weight the author places on overperformance data: predictive but noisy, so use it as a filter rather than a forecast.
insights.quote: Past performance is no guarantee of future political success, but it’s a decent indicator.

insights.claim: Troy Jackson was a consistent electoral overperformer in his Maine State Senate district; that edge diminished somewhat as he became an orthodox progressive on abortion and L.G.B.T. issues, but he still ran very strongly in 2022.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A worked example of the screen in action, and evidence that ideological orthodoxy imposes a measurable electoral cost even on strong retail politicians.
insights.locator: I wrote about Troy Jackson for the New York Times

insights.claim: Rashida Tlaib's electoral performance — roughly neutral in 2020, bad in 2022, a small overperformance in 2024 — is enormously better than Ilhan Omar's, whose four races were all downright terrible with her best still far worse than Tlaib's worst.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that safe-seat members' electoral efficiency varies enormously and goes unpriced — the kind of gap a reformed party would use in promotion decisions.
insights.locator: I don't totally know why Rashida Tlaib's electoral performance

insights.claim: The core institutional failure is accountability, not information: Tlaib gets no credit for her relative overperformance and Omar faces no pressure to improve, despite a genuinely enormous gap.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains why the overperformance rule isn't already used — party incentives don't reward it, so expect slow adoption.
insights.quote: but I wish this was something Tlaib got credit for and Omar faced pressure to work on because the gap is genuinely enormous
insights.locator: but I wish this was something Tlaib got credit for

insights.claim: As Democrats have increasingly become the educated people's party, they have come to badly overrate the literary quality of political speeches relative to their content.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A class-composition explanation for a persistent Democratic messaging weakness — predicts continued mismatch between elite-praised speeches and persuasion of non-college voters.
insights.quote: as Democrats have increasingly become the educated people’s party, they’ve come to really overrate the literary quality of speeches relative to their content

insights.claim: It is not a problem that politicians like Josh Shapiro and Jon Ossoff seem to want to sound like Barack Obama, because Obama was great at speeches — the actual differentiator is that Obama's best speeches said something distinctive.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Redirects the evaluation criterion for 2028 contenders from delivery style to substantive differentiation — the thing that actually correlates with persuasion.
insights.quote: But — and I think this is the important part — Obama’s best speeches actually said something distinctive.
insights.locator: Conversely, I don't think it's the worst thing in the world

insights.claim: Obama's 2004 convention speech asserted that people don't expect government to solve all their problems, that voters resent tax money wasted by a welfare agency or the Pentagon, that parents have to parent and children should turn off television sets, and that the slander of a black youth with a book 'acting white' must be eradicated — content Yglesias says no one in contemporary Democratic Party politics would say today.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Measures how far the party's sayable-idea space has narrowed in 20 years — the substantive gap any 2028 centrist message has to reopen.
insights.quote: I don’t think anyone in contemporary Democratic Party politics would say that today.
insights.locator: This is from Obama's 2004 convention speech

insights.claim: A reader assessment relayed in the post rates Jon Ossoff strong on prepared speeches but dull in informal interviews, AOC the reverse, Josh Shapiro as possibly the best overall combination among likely 2028 contenders, Zohran Mamdani as the most naturally talented at both speeches and interviews, and Pete Buttigieg as articulate but sometimes stiff.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A snapshot of how center-left commentators are ranking the 2028 communication bench, including Mamdani being taken seriously as a national talent.
insights.locator: Matt Bruzunski: Who do you think is the best speaker
